problem: End-to-end deep RL agents (A3C with feed-forward or single-LSTM policies) learn slowly and unstably when navigating large first-person 3D mazes from raw RGB. Rewards are sparse, goals move between episodes, and the agent must localise itself and remember the goal. The only training signal is the sparse RL reward.
motivation: Navigation needs memory at several timescales: one-shot memory of the goal, short-term integration of velocity and vision, and long-term memory of the fixed maze layout. Sparse reward is a poor signal for learning those representations. The authors observe that cheap self-supervised signals available in the simulator carry the geometric and spatial structure navigation needs: depth predicted from RGB, and loop closures computed from integrated velocity. Adding them as auxiliary losses should give denser gradients and speed up representation learning.
key_idea: Augment an A3C agent that has a stacked-LSTM memory and velocity, previous-action and previous-reward inputs with online self-supervised auxiliary losses (depth-band classification from the conv or LSTM features, and loop-closure detection), so that navigation abilities emerge from reward maximisation more quickly and robustly.
insight: Depth works better as a prediction target than as an input: in the appendix, RGBD input performs worse even than depth regression. Classifying depth into 8 non-uniform bands beats MSE regression. Predicting depth from the policy LSTM (D2) beats predicting it from the conv features (D1), giving the best AUC on 3 of 5 mazes in Table 2 (e.g., Random Goal 2 AUC 82.1 vs 66.0 for D1 and 37.0 for plain Nav A3C*). Adding loop closure on top adds little (D1D2L is comparable or slightly worse), and reward prediction à la UNREAL helps less than D2 (RG2 AUC 68.3 vs 82.1). The auxiliary tasks do more than speed up training. The LSTM A3C* baseline trained on 240M frames (score 90, position-decoding accuracy 64.1%) still falls short of Nav A3C+D2 at 120M frames (score 103, accuracy 72.4%). Auxiliary tasks also stabilise learning without reward clipping and make runs more robust to hyperparameters. Linear position-decoding accuracy from the hidden state correlates with score. However, a feed-forward agent is competitive on static mazes (a reactive or wall-following policy stored in the weights), which is why dynamic-goal mazes are needed to test memory.
method: Conv encoder: 2 conv layers (8x8 stride 4 with 16 maps; 4x4 stride 2 with 32 maps) followed by an FC layer over 84x84 RGB, as in the A3C paper.

Nav A3C stacked LSTM: the first LSTM (64 or 128 units) receives conv features plus the previous reward. The second LSTM (256 units) additionally receives the 6-d agent-relative lateral/rotational velocity and the one-hot previous action, and outputs the policy π and value V through separate linear heads.

Depth auxiliary (D1 from conv features, D2 from the top LSTM): a single-layer MLP (128 units) predicts a cropped, subsampled low-resolution depth map as 64 independent 8-way softmaxes. Depth bands are non-uniform after raising depth/255 to the power 10. An MSE regression variant is also tested and performs worse.

Loop-closure auxiliary (L): from the top LSTM, a single-layer MLP with sigmoid/softmax predicts a binary label. The label is 1 if the current position is within η1=1 square of an earlier position and the trajectory went more than η2=2 squares away in between. Positions come from integrating velocity, and training uses a Bernoulli loss.

Training: asynchronous A3C with 16 workers and RMSProp, action repeat 4, and up to 1e8 environment steps. The loss is the A3C gradient plus weighted auxiliary gradients (β_d, β_d', β_l). Auxiliary losses are computed online on the current frame with no replay. For each agent/task, 64 runs are made with randomly sampled hyperparameters and the top 5 are reported.
Analysis tools: a linear position decoder is trained on frozen hidden states over discretised maze cells (50/135/77 locations). tSNE of LSTM cell activations is used in the I-maze.

setting.backbone: Small conv encoder + stacked LSTM (64/128 + 256 units) actor-critic, trained from scratch with A3C
setting.training_data: Online RL in each DeepMind Lab maze (the same maze is used for training and evaluation). Up to 1e8 environment steps (2.5e7 agent steps with action repeat 4) per run, 64 hyperparameter runs per agent/task. Auxiliary targets come from the simulator: Z-buffer depth, and loop-closure labels from integrated velocity.
setting.observation: egocentric 84x84 RGB + 6-d agent-relative velocity + previous action + previous reward (depth used only as a training target)
setting.action_space: 8 discrete actions (small rotations, accelerate forward/backward/sideways, rotational acceleration while moving), action repeat 4
setting.privileged: none at test time beyond odometry-like agent-relative velocity input; GT depth and velocity-integrated positions are used only as training targets

numbers_note: No standard embodied-nav benchmark is used; all results are on DeepMind Lab mazes where training and evaluation happen in the same environment, so split='test' is a convention. Learning curves (Fig. 3), reward-clipping and depth-input comparisons (Fig. 7), non-navigation tasks (Fig. 8) and hyperparameter robustness (Fig. 9) appear only in figures. Table 1 'Goals' printed as x/100 is recorded as the count x. 'Latency 1:>1' printed as e.g. '8.8s:2.5s' is split into Latency1/LatencyN in seconds. Table 2 also gives AUCs for Nav A3C+D1, Nav A3C+D1D2, Nav A3C*+R and Nav A3C+RD2 (e.g., RD2 is best on Static 1 at 105.1 and Random Goal 1 at 72.3); these are omitted here. Text/table inconsistency: the appendix text says LSTM A3C* position accuracy goes 'from 33.4% to 66.5%', but Table 3 prints 64.1.
results: The Nav A3C+D2 agent (stacked LSTM plus depth classification from the policy LSTM) exceeds expert-human score on Static 1 and Static 2 (125% and 116%) and reaches 91% and 59% of human score on Random Goal 1 and 2. On every maze it far outperforms FF A3C* and LSTM A3C* (e.g., RG2 AUC 82.1 vs 50.0 and 37.5; RG1 PosAcc 85.5 vs ~51). Auxiliary tasks roughly double learning-curve AUC over plain Nav A3C* (e.g., Static 2: 157.6 vs 59.9). Depth prediction from the LSTM beats UNREAL-style reward prediction (e.g., I-Maze AUC 203.5 vs 128.2).
limitations: Agents are trained and evaluated on the same fixed maze layouts; there is no generalisation to unseen environments, and the stacked LSTM's limited rapid-memory capacity would struggle in procedurally generated mazes (acknowledged by the authors).

Very sample-hungry RL (up to 1e8 environment steps and 64 hyperparameter runs per configuration, with the top 5 reported). Auxiliary labels depend on simulator-provided depth and velocity, and the agent receives odometry-like velocity as input.
No comparison against SLAM/mapping-based navigation, and results on the largest random-goal maze are still well below human (59%) with no latency improvement after the first goal.
